newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Israel signs nuclear test ban treaty.
newsitem.headline: Israel signs nuclear test ban treaty.

text.p: Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy, whose country is widely believed to have a nuclear weapons programme, signed on Wednesday the Comprehensive Test Ban Treaty (CTBT) banning all nuclear test explosions.

The treaty, approved by the General Assembly Sept. 10, was opened for signature on Tuesday when U.S. President Bill Clinton and the foreign ministers of the four other declared nuclear powers -- Russia, China, Britain and France -- all signed. It has now been signed by more than 70 countries.
A statement issued by Israel's U.N. mission said Israel supported the text of treaty "even though it does not address Israel's concerns and interests in their entirety."
"Israel reconfirms that its support for the CTBT does not reflect any change whatsoever in its policy on the nuclear issue," the statement said. "This policy remains unchanged."
Israel declines to confirm or deny it has a nuclear capability but says it will not be the first to introduce nuclear weapons into the Middle East.

The CTBT will not enter into force until all 44 countries with nuclear reactors have signed and ratified it. India, which is one of them, has said it will not do so. But even before the treaty takes effect it creates an international norm against nuclear test explosions.
